_comment: Raw copy of what the Figma MCP returned for the Playground sections '1. Extent', '2. Condition', '3. Disturbance and Recovery' (file OIsCHIyqMGewUMMOFlbMpr). Read by build-stakeholders.py. Source typos are kept here on purpose; the script fixes them in the output.

extent.title: Extent of mangrove
extent.description: Areas where mangrove was converted to another land use, or gained through planting

condition.title: Condition (of ecosystem)
condition.description: Signals about the state of remaining mangrove and its environment (water, fauna, pollution)

disturbance.title: Disturbancy and recovery
disturbance.description: Abrupt die-off with the site remaining wetland, and whether and how it recovered

labels.note: lowest layer, hidden under the map image

rows: All of ciénaga in Sisal Coast
Plants dying from lack of water; ciénaga drier than before
Less rain, especially inland, so less water reaching the coast underground
ET2: the mangrove used to fill up much more; now plants are dying because not enough water reaches them.
CR2: a year ago the ciénaga was completely dry; now there is some water again.
Trees weakened before dying; pests appearing
CR1: as the water became very salty after Hurricane Gilbert created a lot of breaches, the mangrove began to die, and pests spread through the weakened trees, as in an epidemic.
Water flow blocked near Chuburná due to barrier built in ciénaga
CR2: in the 1980s and 1990s there was plenty of shrimp and crab; now there is almost none.
ET2: a barrier built near Chuburná (neighbouring town) stopped the water flowing in, and the shrimp never came back.

ET2: birds that used to be easy to find on the dune disappeared once people started building this large hotel and because of increased boat traffic from foreign (Canadian) landowners whose property now borders the mangrove.
Waste in the mangrove; dead crocodiles found
Waste from the village and fishers; cause of crocodile deaths unknown
CR1: waste from the village ends up in the mangrove; the mud used to smell clearly polluted.
CR2: a resident found several dead crocodiles without a clear cause (hearsay).
GOV1: Sisal in particular faces other challenges, such as solid waste management; sometimes this waste ends up in illegal dumps in the mangrove zone.
Red tide with high nitrogen; month without income
Possibly wastewater from hotels and farms
NGO1: last year's red tide carried a lot of nitrogen, likely from hotel and farm waste; for a month there was no tourism or fishing.
Risk of wastewater leaking towards the mangrove
Wastewater tanks buried in permeable, flood-prone ground
NGO1: hotels treat their waste in tanks, but in a flood zone with rising water these could leak into the very permeable ground next to the mangroves.

CR1: sites that can handle about ten visitors a day now receive up to 200, often swimming with sunscreen which is very polluting for mangrove water quality. "nature tourism" visitors often have no idea what the ecosystem actually contains and what part people do take within them.
Increased filled up parts of land
Local residents illegaly filling land and selling lots to foreigners
ET2: he describes people without legitimate claims "stealing" land, clearing vegetation, and then selling it on to Canadian buyers.
CR1: whatever happens inland, such as pig and poultry farms, eventually ends up here.
Pollution of mangrove, clearing mangrove for tourism purposes

AC1: Inland, new suburbs are being built between Hunucma and Sisal. These constructions will not only block inland water to reach the Sisal mangroves, but will also increase touristic pressure on them.
AC1: because of local road construction this area totally dried up.
Sisal’s village edge against the mangrove
Landfill for housing as the village grows
CR2: the houses now standing against the ciénaga were built on mangrove that was filled in.
NGO1: residents keep filling land and moving further into the mangrove, even though building on water makes them vulnerable to flooding.
Residents filling land to sell as lots, illegally
NGO1: you can't see it from the street, but people from Sisal cut tall mangrove there, fill the land and sell the lots; in her view this is where the mangrove is currently hit hardest.
Tourism and real estate after the Pueblo Mágico designation
ET1: over the past five years, hotels and beach clubs have been built in the mangrove and behind the dune.
CR2: this construction is for tourism, it’s not housing for locals.
NGO1: since Sisal was announced as Pueblo Mágico, investors in luxury hotels have arrived, fragmenting the dune.
Construction of a very large hotel
NGO1: for a very large hotel, mangrove was cleared and the dune damaged; a protected plant species had to be relocated.
Expected loss: subdivided, not yet cleared
Real estate; change of reserve boundaries
CR2: the whole strip has been divided into lots, and she expects it to be cleared, filled and built on.
NGO1: the area used to lie within the state reserve, but in 2014 the governor changed the decree and the protection was lifted.
ET1: this area will likely disappear as well because of construction work.
Expected loss: subdivided, next to mangrove water
CR2: where she used to collect firewood until recently, the land is now divided into lots, less than 100 m from mangrove water, which she expects will be filled in too.
CR1: this restoration was in 1998, at the location Tzintzin.
Lugar Carbonera (la reserva de ciénagas y manglares)
CR1: These restorations are from 1999, at the location Carbonera.
CR1: I’m not sure about this one, but this was in 1998 or 1999.
CR1: Here after 2000, on both sides of the road between Hunucma and Sisal.
CR1: Here we did plant canals and seedlings 3 years ago.
Hurricane Gilbert: breach, seawater intrusion, areas dried out

NGO1: from her grandparents' stories: much of the mangrove in the ejido zone died or fell. Without trees for shade, a tall grass took over and has prevented mangrove from returning. At La Carbonera, seawater intrusion after the hurricane dried out areas that used to be mangrove.
ET2: The biggest breach hurricane Gilbert gave was in this area close by la carbonera
ET1: Some of the channels the hurricane opened never closed, like "la bocana la carbonera”.
Area behind the Sisal to Mérida road
Die-off due to blocked water flow because of road construction +  Huricanne Gilbert

AC1: in northern Yucatán, roads and harbours that block water flow are the main cause of mangrove degradation. The construction of the road from Hunucma to Sisal blocked waterflow and caused the death of this large area. Huricanne Gilbert amplified this die-off. In the past years we have restored a part of this area.
Hurricane Gilbert: breaches, seawater intrusion, hypersalinity, mass die-off
None for ~8 years; bare zones persist today
Partially naturally, then assisted from 1996 (spring clearing, planting 1997 to 2001)

CR1: the hurricane hit Sisal hard and opened many breaches in the coastal strip, letting in a lot of seawater. The water became hypersaline, the mangrove started dying, pests followed, and around 90% died. Patches of dead trees were visible by 1990. He sees the hurricane as the indirect cause; the real damage came from the rise in salinity.
NGO1: her family recalls that much of the mangrove died or fell after Gilbert; without trees for shade, a tall grass took over and prevented mangrove from returning.
ET1: seawater mixed with the mangrove water, the salt killed the trees, and those zones are still bare today.
Area behind the Sisal to Mérida road
Die-off due to blocked water flow because of road construction +  Huricanne Gilbert

AC1: in northern Yucatán, roads and harbours that block water flow are the main cause of mangrove degradation. The construction of the road from Hunucma to Sisal blocked waterflow and caused the death of this large area. Huricanne Gilbert amplified this die-off. In the past years we have restored a part of this area.
Ciénaga as a whole (no specific location)
Storms Cristóbal, Delta and Zeta: long flooding, possibly salt die-off
Within ~1 year according to one source
CR2: around 2020, during the pandemic, the ciénaga rose and the road between the sea and the ciénaga flooded, after which the water dropped again. She doesn't name the storm specifically.

NGO1: Cristobal, Delta and Zeta brought a lot of rain. Everything was full of water, roadside channels connected to the mangrove and the main road was flooded. She isn't sure whether it was good or bad for the mangrove, or where the water went.
ET2: lot of seawater came in and caused flooding. The mangrove became too salty and died, but re-established within about a year. A breach opened by the storms has since closed again.
CR1: since a barrier now keeps out the sea, storms no longer cause major change.
GOV1: due to heavy rainfall the groundwater rose and the mangrove zones were flooded for five to six months.
